title: Fox out of the Box
bodyHtml:
Zorro the fox is looking for his friend Mapache the raccoon, who likes to hang out in houses where humans live. The following picture shows the fox's search through the house and its surroundings.

Below, sentences in Totonac describe the numbered phases of the search.

Although we've given English descriptions to clarify the drawings, don't assume that the Totonac sentences are direct translations of the English sentences. The sentences in both languages describe the fox's journey, but different languages can focus on different aspects of a scene.

Notes:

  • In the Totonac sentences, a colon “:” indicates a long vowel. The word “n” is added to sentences based on phrasal prosody (making the sound flow well). It doesn't have a meaning (but you are still responsible for using it correctly in your answers).
  • This problem features the variety of Totonac spoken in the town of Zongozotla, Mexico.
  1. Tanu:yi kchiki wa:qni’
    The fox goes into the house through the front door.
  2. Akpu:tukuta n chiki wa:qni’
    The fox comes out of the chimney.
  3. Akpu:tanu:yi n chiki wa:qni’
    The fox enters the house through a hole in the roof.
  4. Cha:qe:taxtiyi n chiki wa:qni’
    The fox comes out the back door.
  5. Lakpa:tuju:yi n chiki wa:qni’
    The fox goes into a flower box on the side of the house.
  6. Tampi:tanu:yi n chiki wa:qni’
    The fox goes under the house.
  7. Tampi:taxtiyi n chiki wa:qni’
    The fox comes out from under the house.
  8. Tuju:yi ktaqalhwaxni wa:qni’
    The fox goes into a hole.
  9. Tukuta ktaqalhwaxni wa:qni’
    The fox comes out of a hole.

assets.alt: Line drawing of a house on stilts, with a fox drawn at nine numbered places: 1 entering the front door, 2 on top of the chimney, 3 coming through a hole in the roof, 4 at a window in the front wall, 5 in a flower box on the side wall, 6 under the house, 7 coming out from under the porch, 8 standing beside the house, 9 in a hole in the ground.

questions.partPrompt: Construct Totonac sentences describing each of these events.
questions.promptHtml: 10. The fox comes out the front door.
12. The fox comes out a hole in the roof.
13. The fox comes in the back door.
14. The fox goes into a window on the side of the house.
15. The fox comes out of a flower box on the back of the house.

hints.text: Every sentence has the same shape: one long verb, then a place word (chiki 'house' or taqalhwaxni 'hole'), then wa:qni’ 'fox'. All the interesting information is packed into the front of the verb, so line the nine verbs up under each other and compare their beginnings and endings.

Each verb splits into a prefix (akpu:, cha:qe:, lakpa:, tampi:, or nothing) that names which part of the house the fox uses, plus a root that says both 'in vs. out' AND what kind of space is involved: one pair of roots is used for entering/leaving a big enclosure, a different pair for entering/leaving a narrow opening such as a hole, a chimney or a box. Also watch what happens to the place word: when the verb carries a prefix, chiki appears as 'n chiki'; when the verb has no prefix, the place word gets a k- glued on front.

Practice on a sentence that isn't asked for: 'The fox comes out of a flower box on the side of the house.' Sentence 5 shows that a flower box on the side is lakpa: + the 'narrow opening' root, and sentences 8-9 show that the 'out' partner of tuju:yi is tukuta. So the verb is lakpa:tukuta, and because the verb has a prefix the rest of the sentence is 'n chiki wa:qni’'.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: Find the skeleton of the sentence

Every Totonac sentence here has exactly the same three-part shape:

VERB   PLACE   wa:qni’

wa:qni’ is at the end of all nine sentences and 'fox' is in all nine English translations, so wa:qni’ = 'fox' (the subject comes last). chiki shows up whenever the house is involved, and taqalhwaxni only in sentences 8 and 9, which mention a hole. So chiki = 'house', taqalhwaxni = 'hole'.

Everything else — door vs. roof vs. under, in vs. out — is crammed into the single long verb at the front. That is very common in languages of Mexico: a lot of what English does with prepositions (into, out of, under, through), Totonac does with pieces glued onto the verb (that's morphology: word-building).

Step 2: Split the verbs into prefix + root

Write the nine verbs in a column:

#verbprefixrootmeaning
1tanu:yi—tanu:yiin, front door
2akpu:tukutaakpu:tukutaout of chimney
3akpu:tanu:yiakpu:tanu:yiin through roof hole
4cha:qe:taxtiyicha:qe:taxtiyiout the back door
5lakpa:tuju:yilakpa:tuju:yiinto side flower box
6tampi:tanu:yitampi:tanu:yiin under the house
7tampi:taxtiyitampi:taxtiyiout from under
8tuju:yi—tuju:yiinto a hole
9tukuta—tukutaout of a hole

Step 3: What the prefixes mean

Comparing 3 (roof) and 2 (chimney, which sticks out of the roof) gives akpu: = 'on top / through the top'. Sentence 4 (back door) gives cha:qe: = 'at the back'. Sentence 5 (side of the house) gives lakpa: = 'on the side / on the wall surface'. Sentences 6 and 7 give tampi: = 'underneath'. And sentences 1, 8, 9 have no prefix: with no prefix you get the default, unmarked route — the front door of a house, or just a plain hole.

Step 4: The two pairs of roots (the tricky part)

There are four roots, and they clearly pair up:

  • tanu:yi 'go in' pairs with taxtiyi 'come out' (both start ta-)
  • tuju:yi 'go in' pairs with tukuta 'come out' (both start tu-)

Why two pairs? Look at what kind of space the fox is moving in and out of:

  • tanu:yi / taxtiyi are used when the fox enters or leaves a big roomy space you can be inside: the house (1, 3, 4) or the open area under the house (6, 7).
  • tuju:yi / tukuta are used for squeezing into or out of a narrow opening or small container: a hole in the ground (8, 9), the chimney tube (2), a flower box (5).

So the root tells you two things at once: direction (in/out) and type of space (roomy vs. narrow). This is the part where English and Totonac 'focus on different aspects of the scene', exactly as the introduction warns.

Step 5: k- and n

Look at the place word. When the verb has no prefix, the place word carries a k-: kchiki (1), ktaqalhwaxni (8, 9). When the verb does have a prefix, the noun appears as plain chiki with the meaningless prosodic filler n in front of it: n chiki. So once you decide on your prefix, the ending of the sentence is decided too:

  • no prefix means k+place, then wa:qni’
  • prefix means n chiki wa:qni’

Step 6: Building the answers

  • 10. out the front door: front door = no prefix; leaving the house (roomy) = taxtiyi; no prefix means kchiki, giving taxtiyi kchiki wa:qni’
  • 11. into the chimney: top = akpu:; entering a narrow tube = tuju:yi, giving akpu:tuju:yi n chiki wa:qni’
  • 12. out a hole in the roof: top = akpu:; leaving the house itself (roomy) = taxtiyi — compare sentence 3, which used tanu:yi for going in the same way, giving akpu:taxtiyi n chiki wa:qni’
  • 13. in the back door: back = cha:qe:; entering the house = tanu:yi, giving cha:qe:tanu:yi n chiki wa:qni’
  • 14. into a window on the side: side = lakpa:; a window leads into the house itself, a roomy space, so tanu:yi (not tuju:yi, which sentence 5 used for the little flower box on the same wall), giving lakpa:tanu:yi n chiki wa:qni’
  • 15. out of a flower box on the back: back = cha:qe:; leaving a small container = tukuta, giving cha:qe:tukuta n chiki wa:qni’

Notice how 12 and 14 are the real test: they force you to keep the prefix (which part of the house) separate from the root choice (roomy space vs. narrow opening).
